subject: Banking
title: Check Fraud Through History
description: A fast breakdown of Check Fraud Through History for builders.

hook.text: Frank Abagnale cashed $2.5 million in forged checks before age 21. His story became the film Catch Me If You Can.

buildup.text: Check fraud relies on the delay between deposit and clearing. By the time the fraud is discovered, the thief is gone.

discovery.text: Modern check fraud costs $27 billion annually in the US. Despite digital payments, checks remain a top fraud target.

twist.text: Remote deposit via phone photos created new vulnerabilities. People deposit the same check at multiple banks.

climax.text: Checks survive because businesses trust them. But that trust makes them one of the easiest payment tools to exploit.

punchline.text: $27 billion in annual fraud. Checks are trusted and exploited.

quiz.question: Why are checks still a major fraud target?
options: The clearing delay gives fraudsters time to disappear

details.summary: Check fraud has evolved from simple forgery to sophisticated check-washing, account takeover, and synthetic identity schemes, costing banks billions annually despite the decline of check usage overall.
details.whyItMatters: Check fraud remains one of the most common forms of bank fraud precisely because checks are an old, relatively insecure payment method that millions still use and trust without understanding the risks.
takeaways: Check fraud costs US banks over $20 billion annually
Check washing chemically erases ink to alter payee and amount
Mobile deposit capture has created new duplicate deposit fraud schemes

faq.question: How does check washing work?
faq.answer: Criminals steal checks from mailboxes and use common chemicals like acetone to dissolve the ink. They then rewrite the check to a different payee for a larger amount, depositing it before the victim notices.

faq.question: Why hasn't check fraud been eliminated?
faq.answer: Checks lack the real-time verification of card payments. The clearing process takes days, giving fraudsters a window to cash out. Banks also hesitate to reject checks outright because legitimate check use remains significant.
